topics.topic: Datetime implementation, representable range, and handling of overflow during timezone-to-UTC conversion
questions: Does "can hold" apply only to the camera's parsed local fields, or must the value also remain representable while its offset or configured time zone is applied, it is converted to UTC, and it is compared with the modification time; and which standard-library datetime implementation defines those limits?
Which language and exact datetime type defines representability, including its minimum and maximum values?

Must a camera value also be treated as unusable when applying its offset or configured time zone produces a UTC instant that the required datetime representation cannot hold, and what happens instead if that conversion overflows?
Which standard library, datetime type and version define the accepted range, and does “can hold” test only the parsed wall-clock fields or the timezone-resolved UTC instant as well?
What happens when the parsed local camera date is representable but applying its EXIF or run-timezone offset produces a UTC instant outside the datetime type's representable range?

quotes:
3. The photo moment is the first usable value of: EXIF `DateTimeOriginal`, EXIF `DateTime`, then
   the file's modification time. `DateTimeOriginal` uses `OffsetTimeOriginal` when that offset matches
   the imported `EXIF_OFFSET_PATTERN` constant whole, with hours up to the imported `CAMERA_OFFSET_MAX_HOURS` constant and minutes that are a minute of the hour; otherwise it is read in the time zone of the `timezone` field of the run settings (A8), and so is
   `DateTime`. A camera value is unusable when it does not match the imported `EXIF_DATETIME_PATTERN` constant whole or is no date and time the standard library's datetime type can hold, so a leap second is unusable, when its UTC year
   is before the imported `CAMERA_EARLIEST_YEAR` constant, or when it is more than the imported
   `CAMERA_LATEST_AFTER_MODIFIED_HOURS` constant of hours after the file's modification time.

4. The photo date is delivered as UTC without an offset, as the Client Portal stores it. A camera
   time with no offset is read in the time zone of that `timezone` field. A local time that occurs twice is the
   first occurrence, and a local time that does not exist is read with the offset in force before
   the clock change. A modification time is an absolute instant converted to UTC.
judgement.divergence: One implementation treats overflow while resolving or converting a locally representable camera value as making that value unusable and falls through to the next photo-moment source; another treats the local value as usable and lets UTC conversion fail, so the calling flow observes a successful placement with a fallback date versus an operation failure.
judgement.why: The holdability clause does not say whether representability must survive timezone resolution and UTC conversion or what outcome conversion overflow has.

witness.initial: A decodable source has `DateTimeOriginal` 9999-12-31 23:30:00, an accepted `OffsetTimeOriginal` of -01:00, a usable `DateTime` fallback, and a modification time that does not independently reject the original value.
events: The calling flow asks the deliverer to place the source photo.
The deliverer parses the locally representable `DateTimeOriginal` and applies its accepted offset, producing a mathematical UTC instant in year 10000.
outcomes: The conversion overflow makes `DateTimeOriginal` unusable, so the deliverer uses `DateTime` and returns a placement with that fallback photo date.
The locally representable `DateTimeOriginal` remains selected, UTC conversion overflows, and the delivery fails without a specified placement failure or fallback.
witness.observer: The calling flow sees either a successful placement with a fallback photo date or an operation failure.
basis:
The deliverer offers three operations: scan a project's folder, deliver one photo, and record its
publication.

3. One call delivers one photo, named by `name`, a relative path in the form a scan reports, and
   `source_id`. The service keeps no memory of earlier scans: it judges the name and the file when the call
   runs.

3. The photo moment is the first usable value of: EXIF `DateTimeOriginal`, EXIF `DateTime`, then
   the file's modification time.

topics.topic: Valid OffsetTimeOriginal minute-field values and handling of out-of-range values
questions: Which numeric minute values make OffsetTimeOriginal usable, including the exact lower and upper bounds?
What exact minute values are accepted, and must values outside that set make the offset unusable rather than be accepted or normalized by an offset parser?
Which numeric minute-field values are valid, especially `00` and `60`?

quotes:
`DateTimeOriginal` uses `OffsetTimeOriginal` when that offset matches
   the imported `EXIF_OFFSET_PATTERN` constant whole, with hours up to the imported `CAMERA_OFFSET_MAX_HOURS` constant and minutes that are a minute of the hour; otherwise it is read in the time zone of the `timezone` field of the run settings (A8), and so is
   `DateTime`.
judgement.why: A numeric minute of the hour is 00 through 59, so 00 is accepted, 60 is not, and an offset with an invalid minute field is not used.

topics.topic: Handling an unrepresentable file modification time during comparison or fallback
questions: What must the delivery do when the file modification instant cannot be represented by the required datetime form, either while comparing a camera value with it or when using it as the fallback photo moment?

quotes:
3. The photo moment is the first usable value of: EXIF `DateTimeOriginal`, EXIF `DateTime`, then
   the file's modification time.
A modification time is an absolute instant converted to UTC.

4. A file's modification time is converted to the same form before it is compared or delivered, dropping
   any fraction finer than a microsecond toward the earlier instant.
judgement.why: The unchanged rules already made file modification time the mandatory fallback and required its UTC conversion, while the change since closure only refined camera datetime and offset validation and did not make modification-time representability newly relevant.
